mcqs.question: A document-sharing product needs "anyone this doc was shared with, or a member of a group it's shared with" to determine access. Which model fits that requirement most naturally?
options: ReBAC, since access follows a relationship graph rather than a fixed role or attribute rule
RBAC, since sharing is just another role like "editor"
ABAC, since group membership is an attribute of the user
None of these models can express sharing — it needs custom code outside any of them
mcqs.explanation: This requirement is fundamentally a graph traversal — direct shares, group membership, and nested folders all chain together — which is exactly what ReBAC models. RBAC's static roles and ABAC's attribute rules can approximate parts of this but get unwieldy fast; it doesn't require bespoke code outside a permission model.

mcqs.question: Why do most production systems use a policy-engine library embedded in every service, rather than a pure network-call-per-check PDP or fully independent per-service logic?
options: It's the only approach that supports RBAC
It gets consistency from one centrally-owned rule set without paying a network hop on every request
It removes the need for a PDP altogether
mcqs.explanation: Embedding the same policy engine everywhere, fed by one central rule source, gives every service the same answer without a per-request network call — the best of both approaches. It works with any authorization model, doesn't preclude caching, and there's usually still a central place rules are managed even if evaluation is distributed.

mcqs.question: A team caches permission decisions for 60 seconds to hit their latency budget. What real risk does that introduce?
options: The cache will run out of memory under any realistic load
A permission revoked mid-window can still appear valid to the cache until it expires
Caching decisions is never safe for any kind of permission check
It eliminates the need for a policy decision point entirely
mcqs.explanation: Caching trades correctness for speed — the TTL is really a statement about how much staleness the system accepts, so a revoked permission can still read as valid until the cache clears. Memory exhaustion isn't the inherent risk, caching is fine for low-stakes checks, and it doesn't remove the need for a PDP, just reduces how often it's called.

mcqs.question: Ten services each implement their own version of "can this user edit this resource," and they've quietly drifted apart. What is the correct fix?
options: Have each team write more unit tests for their own implementation
Rewrite every service to be a monolith
Give every service its own dedicated database to avoid conflicts
Centralize the rules in one policy engine or library so every service evaluates the same logic, even if evaluation itself stays distributed
mcqs.explanation: More tests per service can't catch drift between services, since there's no single implementation being tested against. The fix is treating authorization as a shared concern with one rule source. This isn't about databases or reverting to a monolith — it's about where the permission logic itself lives.
